hook.text: A capuchin monkey receives a cucumber slice. She is content. Then she sees her neighbor receive a grape.

buildup.text: Inequity aversion means preferring fairness over higher personal payoff. Both getting less and getting more can feel.

discovery.text: Fehr and Schmidt modeled two types: disadvantageous inequity aversion, disliking having less, and advantageous.

twist.text: Advantageous inequity aversion is weaker. People dislike receiving less far more than they dislike receiving more.

climax.text: Inequity aversion shapes salary negotiations, taxes, and redistribution policy.

punchline.text: Fairness matters so much we sacrifice to achieve it.

quiz.question: What did the capuchin monkey experiment reveal?
options: Monkeys prefer grapes to cucumbers for nutritional reasons
Even primates reject unequal treatment, showing inequity aversion

details.summary: Inequity aversion is the preference for fair outcomes where people dislike both earning less than others (disadvantageous inequity) and earning more than others (advantageous inequity), though the former is felt more strongly.
details.whyItMatters: Inequity aversion explains why people reject profitable but unequal offers, why wage compression exists within firms, and why perceived unfairness triggers strikes, protests, and social unrest even when absolute conditions are adequate.
takeaways: People dislike both being worse off and being better off than others
Disadvantageous inequity causes stronger negative feelings than advantageous
Fehr-Schmidt model formalizes inequity aversion mathematically

faq.question: Why would someone dislike earning more than others?
faq.answer: Advantageous inequity triggers guilt and social discomfort. People often voluntarily share windfalls, leave larger tips for poorer servers, and support redistribution policies because being unfairly advantaged creates psychological cost.

faq.question: How does inequity aversion affect workplace behavior?
faq.answer: Workers who discover colleagues earn more for similar work reduce effort or quit, even if their own pay is fair in absolute terms. This explains why pay transparency can backfire if inequities exist across roles.
